text: Which one of the following well-formed formulae is a tautology? (A) ∀x∃y R(x,y) ↔ ∃y∀x R(x,y) (B) (∀x[∃y R(x,y) → S(x,y)]) → ∀x∃y S(x,y) (C) [∀x∃y(P(x,y)→R(x,y))] ↔ [∀x∃y(¬P(x,y)∨R(x,y))] (D) ∀x∀y P(x,y) → ∀x∀y P(y,x)
solution: The propositional part of this first-order question is that P→R ≡ ¬P∨R inside the quantifier scope. Replacing P(x,y)→R(x,y) by ¬P(x,y)∨R(x,y) on the left makes both sides literally identical, so the formula has the propositional form A↔A, a tautology in PL. Options (A) and (D) swap/permute quantifiers and predicate arguments; (B) fails when R and S are both false everywhere.
source_label: GATE Overflow question page for GATE CS 2015 Set 2 Q.55 with the accepted solution by Deepak Poonia, which reduces the first-order formula to the propositional tautology A <-> A
answer_evidence: Now, we can take $A = [\forall x \exists y( \neg P(x,y) \vee R(x,y))]$ and so $A \leftrightarrow A$ is tautology in PL.
